# Adopt a layer

Add a practice to this repository as a versioned, removable unit.

## When

Somebody asks to adopt, install or try a layer; somebody links to one; or you are
deciding whether a published layer is worth taking on.

## Look before you adopt

```
ilk info <ref>
```

A reference is a built-in name (`record`), a path (`./layers/mine`), or a git source
(`gh:owner/repo@v1`, `gh:owner/repo/layers/name@v1`).

Read four things, in this order:

1. **What it writes, and in which mode.** `managed` files are the layer's; `region`
   blocks live inside files that stay yours; `create-only` files are seeded and then
   handed over. A layer claiming `managed` on a file your team edits will fight you
   every upgrade — that is the single most common reason a layer is wrong for a repo.
2. **Its instruction budget.** Always-on instructions are in every context window
   forever. `ilk info` shows the declared cost; if the repository is near its ceiling,
   adopting is a decision about what to give up.
3. **What it requires.** An unmet capability is not fatal — the layer adopts and its
   dependent checks skip — but you will get no value until you supply it.
4. **Whether it runs code.** `ilk info` says so plainly. See below.

## Adopting

```
ilk adopt <ref>                                   # shows the plan, asks before writing
ilk adopt <ref> --set test.command="go test ./..."  # supply a capability at the same time
ilk adopt <ref> --var docs_dir=documentation        # override a layer variable
ilk adopt <ref> --no-apply                          # print the plan and write nothing
```

**Read the plan before answering.** It lists every file, every fenced block, and every
refusal. This is the moment the whole blast radius is visible, and it is cheap to look.

If the plan touches something you did not expect, decline and ask why rather than
adopting and cleaning up afterwards.

## Layers that run code

A layer from a source ilk did not ship, that carries scripts, command-based checks or
subcommands, will refuse to adopt without consent:

```
ilk adopt gh:someone/theirs --allow-exec
```

Do not pass that flag reflexively. Read the scripts first — `ilk info` names them, and
the source is a git repository you can open. A declarative layer needs no consent at
all, because `ilk plan` shows every byte before anything is written; the flag exists
precisely to mark the difference.

If you are adopting on somebody else's behalf and the layer needs `--allow-exec`, say
so and let them decide. Consent is not yours to give.

## After adopting

```
ilk check     # the layer's checks now run; some may fail immediately
ilk brief     # confirm the new skills and commands are visible to a session
```

New checks failing straight away is normal and not a reason to panic — the layer is
telling you what the repository does not yet satisfy. Fix them or, if the layer turns
out to be wrong for this project:

```
ilk drop <name>
```

Everything it added is removed. Anything you edited afterwards is left alone, and
files it merely seeded stay yours. Trying a layer is meant to be cheap; that is the
whole point of the ownership modes.

## What not to do

- Do not hand-write the layer's files instead of adopting it. You lose the upgrade
  path, and `ilk check` will report the result as drift for ever.
- Do not adopt several layers at once when evaluating. One at a time, with `ilk check`
  in between, tells you which one caused what.
- Do not pass `--force` to make an adoption fit. A conflict at adoption time means the
  layer wants a file that already exists and is not ilk's — decide deliberately.
